steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine learning paper that proposes a simulation-free training objective for the Schrödinger bridge problem, based on score and flow matching. Motivate it from the limitations of diffusion and flow-based models, review existing Schrödinger bridge methods, and summarize our method, experiments (including single-cell data) and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Score-based generative models and their Gaussian-source assumption
- Flow-based models (CNFs) and simulation-free objectives
- The Schrödinger bridge problem and existing solvers
- Our method: [SF] 2 M
- Experiments: synthetic data and single-cell dynamics
- Summary of contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Score-based generative models (SBGMs)
  - incl. diffusion models; represent complex distributions over high-dim spaces (cite)
  - sample by simulating evolution of source density (nearly always Gaussian) under an SDE (cite)
  - restricted by Gaussian source assumption, essential for simulation-free denoising objective
  - assumption often violated for temporal evolution of physical/biological systems, e.g. single-cell gene expression -> can't learn underlying dynamics
- Flow-based models
  - approach of choice; = continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) (cite)
  - deterministic continuous-time generative process; fit ODE transforming source to target density
  - previously limited by inefficient simulation-based training (expensive ODE integration at training time)
  - recent simulation-free objectives: CNFs competitive with SBGMs for Gaussian source (cite); extended to arbitrary sources (cite)
  - but: no stochastic dynamics -- useful for generative modeling and recovering system dynamics
- Schrödinger bridge (SB) problem
  - canonical probabilistic formulation of stochastic mapping between two arbitrary distributions
  - most likely evolution between source and target under a reference process (cite)
  - applications: generative modeling, natural stochastic dynamical systems, mean field games (cite each)
  - no closed form except special cases (e.g. Gaussian) (cite)
  - iterative algorithms that simulate the learned stochastic process (cite); numerical/practical issues, poor scaling to high dimensions (cite)
- Our method: simulation-free score and flow matching ([SF] 2 M)
  - first simulation-free objective for SB
  - generalizes (1) simulation-free CNF objectives (cite) to stochastic dynamics, (2) diffusion denoising objective to arbitrary sources (Fig. 1)
  - SB <-> entropic OT: SB as mixture of Brownian bridges (cite)
  - static entropic OT maps via Sinkhorn (cite) instead of simulating an SDE every iteration as dynamic SB algorithms do
- Experiments
  - synthetic: beats related prior work, better approximation to true SB
  - real data: cross-sectional measurements (unpaired time series) as a sequence of SBs
  - prior cell SB methods: static (cite) or low-dim dynamic (cite); ours first to scale to thousands of gene dimensions (fully simulation-free training)
  - static manifold geodesic map -> better cell interpolations; one of first practical SB approximations with non-Euclidean costs
  - unlike static OT: recover gene-gene interaction network driving cell dynamics
- Contributions
  - [SF] 2 M, first simulation-free SB objective, proof of correctness
  - empirical + minibatch approximations to entropic OT plan
  - validation on synthetic distributions + several single-cell dynamics problems

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Score-based generative models (SBGMs), which include diffusion models, are a powerful class of generative models and they can represent complex distributions over high-dimensional spaces. To generate samples, SBGMs usually simulate how a source density evolves under a stochastic differential equation (SDE), and the source density is nearly always a Gaussian. SBGMs work well empirically, but they are restricted because they assume a Gaussian source, and this assumption is essential for optimizing them with the simulation-free denoising objective. In the temporal evolution of physical or biological systems this assumption is often violated, for example in single-cell gene expression data, and so SBGMs can't be used there to learn the underlying dynamics.

For problems like these, flow-based generative models have been an approach of choice; these are synonymous with continuous normalizing flows (CNFs). Flow-based models assume that the generative process is deterministic and continuous in time, and they fit an ordinary differential equation (ODE) which transforms the source density into the target density. Before, flow-based models were limited because their training objectives were simulation-based and inefficient, needing an expensive integration of the ODE at training time. Recent work has introduced simulation-free training objectives that make CNFs competitive with SBGMs when the source is Gaussian, and these objectives were also extended to arbitrary source distributions. But these objectives still do not apply to learning stochastic dynamics, which can be beneficial for generative modeling and also for recovering the dynamics of systems.

The Schrödinger bridge (SB) problem considers the most likely evolution between a source and a target probability distribution under a given reference process. It is the canonical probabilistic formulation of mapping stochastically between two arbitrary distributions. The SB problem has been applied to many kinds of problems, such as generative modeling, modeling natural stochastic dynamical systems, and mean field games. Apart from a few special cases (for example the Gaussian case), the SB problem usually does not have a closed-form solution. It can be approximated with iterative algorithms, but these need to simulate the learned stochastic process. These methods are sound in theory, but they have numerical and practical issues that limit how well they scale to high dimensions.

- Our method: simulation-free score and flow matching ([SF] 2 M)
  - first simulation-free objective for SB
  - generalizes (1) simulation-free CNF objectives to stochastic dynamics, (2) diffusion denoising objective to arbitrary sources (Fig. 1)
  - SB <-> entropic OT: SB as mixture of Brownian bridges
  - static entropic OT maps via Sinkhorn instead of simulating an SDE every iteration (dynamic SB algorithms)
- Experiments
  - synthetic: beats related prior work, better approximation to true SB
  - real data: cross-sectional measurements (unpaired time series) as a sequence of SBs
  - prior cell SB methods static or low-dim dynamic; ours first to scale to thousands of gene dimensions (simulation-free training)
  - static manifold geodesic map -> better cell interpolations; one of first practical SB approximations with non-Euclidean costs
  - unlike static OT: recover gene-gene interaction network driving cell dynamics
- Contributions
  - [SF] 2 M, first simulation-free SB objective, proof of correctness
  - empirical + minibatch approximations to entropic OT plan
  - validation on synthetic distributions + several single-cell dynamics problems

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Score-based generative models (SBGMs), which include diffusion models, are a powerful class of generative models and they can represent complex distributions over high-dimensional spaces. To generate samples, SBGMs usually simulate how a source density evolves under a stochastic differential equation (SDE), and the source density is nearly always a Gaussian. SBGMs work well empirically, but they are restricted because they assume a Gaussian source, and this assumption is essential for optimizing them with the simulation-free denoising objective. In the temporal evolution of physical or biological systems this assumption is often violated, for example in single-cell gene expression data, and so SBGMs can't be used there to learn the underlying dynamics.

For problems like these, flow-based generative models have been an approach of choice; these are synonymous with continuous normalizing flows (CNFs). Flow-based models assume that the generative process is deterministic and continuous in time, and they fit an ordinary differential equation (ODE) which transforms the source density into the target density. Before, flow-based models were limited because their training objectives were simulation-based and inefficient, needing an expensive integration of the ODE at training time. Recent work has introduced simulation-free training objectives that make CNFs competitive with SBGMs when the source is Gaussian, and these objectives were also extended to arbitrary source distributions. But these objectives still do not apply to learning stochastic dynamics, which can be beneficial for generative modeling and also for recovering the dynamics of systems.

The Schrödinger bridge (SB) problem considers the most likely evolution between a source and a target probability distribution under a given reference process. It is the canonical probabilistic formulation of mapping stochastically between two arbitrary distributions. The SB problem has been applied to many kinds of problems, such as generative modeling, modeling natural stochastic dynamical systems, and mean field games. Apart from a few special cases (for example the Gaussian case), the SB problem usually does not have a closed-form solution. It can be approximated with iterative algorithms, but these need to simulate the learned stochastic process. These methods are sound in theory, but they have numerical and practical issues that limit how well they scale to high dimensions.

In this paper we introduce a simulation-free objective for the Schrödinger bridge problem, which we call simulation-free score and flow matching ([SF] 2 M). [SF] 2 M generalizes two things at the same time: (1) the simulation-free objectives for CNFs, which it generalizes to stochastic dynamics, and (2) the denoising training objective for diffusion models, which it generalizes to arbitrary source distributions (Fig. 1). Our algorithm uses a connection between the SB problem and entropic optimal transport (OT) so that the Schrödinger bridge can be written as a mixture of Brownian bridges. Dynamic SB algorithms have to simulate an SDE at every iteration, but [SF] 2 M instead uses static entropic OT maps between the source and target distributions, and these can be computed efficiently with the Sinkhorn algorithm.

We show that [SF] 2 M is effective on synthetic and on real-world datasets. On the synthetic data, [SF] 2 M does better than related prior work and it finds a better approximation to the true Schrödinger bridge. For real data, we model sequences of cross-sectional measurements (i.e., unpaired time series observations) by a sequence of Schrödinger bridges. There are many prior methods that model cells with Schrödinger bridges in the static setting or in the low-dimensional dynamic setting, but [SF] 2 M is the first method that can scale to thousands of gene dimensions, since its training is completely simulation-free. We also introduce a static manifold geodesic map, and it improves cell interpolations in the dynamic setting, which is one of the first practical applications of Schrödinger bridge approximations with non-Euclidean costs. Finally, we show that unlike with static optimal transport, we can directly model and recover the gene-gene interaction network that drives the cell dynamics.

Our main contributions are:

- We present [SF] 2 M, which is the first simulation-free objective for the Schrödinger bridge problem, and we prove that it is correct.

- We study empirical and minibatch approximations to the entropic OT plan used in [SF] 2 M that work well.

- We validate the method on synthetic distributions and on several single-cell dynamics problems.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Score-based generative models (SBGMs), including diffusion models, are a powerful class of generative models that can represent complex distributions over high-dimensional spaces [1,2,3,4,5]. SBGMs typically generate samples by simulating the evolution of a source density, which is nearly always a Gaussian, according to a stochastic differential equation (SDE) [6]. Despite their empirical success, SBGMs are restricted by their assumption of a Gaussian source, which is essential for optimizing them with the simulation-free denoising objective. This assumption is often violated in the temporal evolution of physical or biological systems, such as single-cell gene expression data, which prevents SBGMs from being used to learn the underlying dynamics.

An approach of choice in such problems has been to use flow-based generative models, which are synonymous with continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) [7,8,9]. Flow-based models assume a deterministic continuous-time generative process and fit an ordinary differential equation (ODE) that transforms the source density into the target density. Flow-based models were previously limited by inefficient simulation-based training objectives requiring an expensive integration of the ODE at training time. However, recent work has introduced simulation-free training objectives that make CNFs competitive with SBGMs when a Gaussian source is assumed [10,11,12], and has extended these objectives to arbitrary source distributions [13,14,15]. Still, these objectives do not yet apply to learning stochastic dynamics, which can be beneficial both for generative modeling and for recovering the dynamics of systems.

The Schrödinger bridge (SB) problem, the canonical probabilistic formulation of stochastically mapping between two arbitrary distributions, considers the most likely evolution between a source and a target probability distribution under a given reference process [16,17]. The SB problem has been applied to a wide variety of problems, including generative modeling [18,19,20,21,2], modeling natural stochastic dynamical systems [22,23,24], and mean field games [25]. Except for a small number of special cases (e.g., Gaussian [26,27]), the SB problem typically has no closed-form solution, but it can be approximated with iterative algorithms that require simulating the learned stochastic process [18,20,27]. While theoretically sound, these methods have numerical and practical issues that limit their scalability to high dimensions [28].

This paper introduces a simulation-free objective for the Schrödinger bridge problem called simulation-free score and flow matching ([SF] 2 M). [SF] 2 M simultaneously generalizes (1) the simulation-free objectives for CNFs [15,11] to stochastic dynamics and (2) the denoising training objective for diffusion models to arbitrary source distributions (Fig. 1). Our algorithm uses a connection between the SB problem and entropic optimal transport (OT) to express the Schrödinger bridge as a mixture of Brownian bridges [18,17]. Unlike dynamic SB algorithms, which require simulating an SDE at every iteration, [SF] 2 M takes advantage of static entropic OT maps between the source and target distributions, which can be computed efficiently by the Sinkhorn algorithm [29].

We demonstrate the effectiveness of [SF] 2 M on both synthetic and real-world datasets. On synthetic data, we show that [SF] 2 M performs better than related prior work and finds a better approximation to the true Schrödinger bridge. As an application to real data, we model sequences of cross-sectional measurements (i.e., unpaired time series observations) by a sequence of Schrödinger bridges. While there are many prior methods that model cells with Schrödinger bridges in the static setting [22,30,31,32] or in the low-dimensional dynamic setting [33,27,24], [SF] 2 M is the first method able to scale to thousands of gene dimensions, because its training is completely simulation-free. We also introduce a static manifold geodesic map that improves cell interpolations in the dynamic setting, one of the first practical applications of Schrödinger bridge approximations with non-Euclidean costs. Finally, we show that, unlike with static optimal transport, we can directly model and recover the gene-gene interaction network driving the cell dynamics.

Our main contributions are summarized below:

- We present [SF] 2 M, the first simulation-free objective for the Schrödinger bridge problem, and prove its correctness.

- We study effective empirical and minibatch approximations to the entropic OT plan used in [SF] 2 M.

- We validate the proposed method on synthetic distributions and in several single-cell dynamics problems.
